Module 03 of 11

Module 3 — Mapping High-Quality Support & Resistance

Zones not lines. Supply and demand, fresh versus tested, flip zones, liquidity around obvious levels, and how false breakouts happen.

3.1What this module gives you

Module 2 gave you the skeleton — swings, trend, BOS, MSS, displacement. This module gives you the places. Support and resistance is where Gate 2 is won or lost, and it is the single most abused concept in retail trading, because a horizontal line is easy to draw and almost impossible to evaluate.

The claim of this module

A zone is not a place where you expect price to turn. It is a place where you have evidence that participants acted before, and a reason to believe unfilled orders remain. Expectation is a feeling. Evidence has a chart location and a mechanism.

By the end of this module you will be able to

  1. Build a zone from price behaviour — bodies, wicks, displacement origin, pre-expansion base — and justify its width without reference to preference.
  2. Score any zone against six criteria before price arrives, so you are not negotiating with yourself while it moves.
  3. Explain why the third touch is weaker than the first, and why the phrase 'a strong level, it's held three times' is backwards.
  4. Identify where liquidity actually rests, and why obvious levels are targets rather than protection.
  5. Distinguish a false breakout from a genuine one using the same close-versus-wick logic from Module 2, plus displacement.
  6. Stack 4H, 1H and 15M zones into a single location rather than mistaking alignment for three separate confirmations.
Prerequisite

Module 2's Practical 2.1 — the Fifty-Pivot Drill must be complete. Every zone in this module is anchored to a structural point. If your pivots are unreliable, your zones will inherit the error — and a drawn rectangle looks authoritative no matter how badly it was derived, which makes the error harder to see, not easier.

3.2Why a line is the wrong tool

The standard retail approach is to find a price where the market turned and draw a horizontal line through it. The line is precise to the pip. That precision is entirely fake, and it fails in a specific, predictable way.

What the line actually does to your decisions

Three concrete failures

  1. It generates false invalidations. Price trades one pip through your line and you conclude support failed. It did not fail; your model of it was too narrow. You then stand aside for the move you correctly anticipated.
  2. It generates false entries. Price touches the line exactly and you enter, even though the actual reaction area was eight pips lower and price has not reached it yet. You are early, and your stop is inside the zone rather than beyond it.
  3. It hides the mechanism. A line says 'price turned here'. A zone says 'price turned here because a displacement leg originated from this area and the orders that created it were never fully filled'. Only the second statement tells you when to stop believing it.
The rule

You never choose a zone's width. You read it off the candles that made the level matter. If you find yourself adjusting a zone's edges to include a reaction that fell outside it, you are no longer analysing — you are fitting.

3.3The four sources of a zone

Every legitimate zone in this system comes from one of four observable price behaviours. Each gives you specific edges, derived from specific candles.

SourceUpper edgeLower edgeWhy it holds orders
Displacement originThe open (or body top) of the last candle before the moveThe low of the consolidation the move launched fromThe move left before all resting orders were filled. Unfilled interest remains at the origin.
Reaction areaThe highest body close among the reaction candlesThe deepest wick of the clusterRepeated defence at a price band means participants keep acting there. The wick span records how far they let it go.
Pre-expansion baseThe high of the consolidationThe low of the consolidationPositions were accumulated across the whole base. Returning to it brings price back to everyone's entry.
Swing areaThe extreme wick of the pivotThe body top (for a high) or body bottom (for a low)The pivot itself is visible to everyone, so it attracts both reaction orders and the stops resting beyond it.
A note on naming

Other frameworks call these order blocks, supply and demand zones, imbalance or fair-value gaps, and points of control. The labels differ; the underlying observation is the same — price left an area quickly, which implies orders there were not fully worked. This course avoids the branded vocabulary deliberately, because the names invite you to trust the pattern rather than the mechanism. If you already use those terms, map them onto the four sources above and keep going.

Zones expire

A zone is a record of past behaviour, and the participants who created it do not stay interested forever. A 1H zone from four sessions ago is materially weaker than one from this morning. A 4H zone holds relevance longer than a 15M one. There is no exact expiry, but the honest default is this: if price has traded through the area since the zone formed, or if the session that created it has ended and two more have passed without a return, treat it as stale and demote it.

Check your understanding
You are marking a 1H demand zone. Price consolidated between 1.0902 and 1.0918 for six candles, then displaced upward, with the final consolidation candle opening at 1.0915 and closing at 1.0917. Where do the zone's edges go?

Correct for this source type. This is a pre-expansion base: price accumulated across the whole six-candle range before committing. Every participant who positioned during that consolidation did so somewhere between 1.0902 and 1.0918, so the entire span is the area that matters. Upper edge from the consolidation high, lower edge from the consolidation low — both read off the chart, neither chosen.

A 16-pip zone is wide for a 1H entry, and that is worth noticing rather than hiding. It directly affects Gate 5: your structural stop must sit below 1.0902 (say 1.0898), so if you enter on a 15M confirmation near 1.0912 your risk is roughly 14 pips and you need 28 pips of structural target to clear 1:2. If the next structural high is only 20 pips away, this zone is correctly drawn and the trade is still rejected. That is the 'width sanity' criterion in §3.6 doing its job.

Note also what you do not do: you do not narrow the zone to make the arithmetic work. Narrowing to 1.0910–1.0918 would produce a prettier R:R and a stop sitting inside the area where price is genuinely likely to trade. Module 1 named this exactly — a tighter stop is a higher loss rate in disguise.

This is the over-precision error, and it is seductive because it feels rigorous. A 2-pip zone looks surgical. What it actually does is reintroduce the thin-line problem from §3.2 wearing a rectangle's clothing.

The reasoning behind this choice is usually 'the last candle before the move is where the aggressor was working'. But the whole six-candle consolidation is where positioning occurred — the final candle is simply the last one before the trigger, not the only one that mattered. Orders were resting throughout the base, and price returning to 1.0905 is returning into that inventory just as much as price returning to 1.0916.

The practical damage is twofold. First, price will frequently trade to 1.0906 and reverse hard without ever touching your 2-pip box, so you miss the trade you correctly identified. Second, if you do get filled, your structural stop is now only a few pips away — below 1.0913, perhaps — which sits inside the consolidation. Normal movement within the base takes you out. You will record this as 'the zone failed'. The zone did not fail; the box did.

You have drawn a zone where nothing happened. The range 1.0918–1.0930 is part of the displacement leg itself — price moved through it quickly and did not consolidate there. There is no accumulation, no repeated reaction, no origin. It is empty space that price happened to travel across.

The intuition being applied is 'price will get there first, so let me catch it earlier'. That is an impatience heuristic, not an analytical one, and it inverts the logic of the system. You are not trying to be filled as early as possible; you are trying to be filled where you have evidence. Entering at 1.0925 means entering with a structural stop that still has to go below 1.0902 — the zone has not moved just because your entry did. Your risk grows by 10 pips while your reward shrinks by 10, which can turn a 1:2.3 into a 1:1.4 and fail Gate 5 outright.

There is one legitimate version of this idea worth distinguishing: if the displacement leg left a genuine imbalance — a gap between candle ranges where no two-way trade occurred — that is a real feature, and it often gets filled. But it is a transit area, not a demand zone, and it does not carry the order-flow argument that makes a zone tradable.

Right instinct, wrong place to express it — and this distinction matters more than it first appears. You are correct that price frequently trades a few pips beyond an obvious low before reversing. Module 2's failed-break work and §3.7 below both cover exactly this. But padding the zone is the wrong response.

The zone and the stop are two different objects doing two different jobs. The zone answers 'where is the evidence of participation?' — that answer is 1.0902 to 1.0918, determined by the candles. The stop answers 'at what price is my thesis disproven?' — and that is where the sweep allowance belongs, which is why a structural stop goes below the zone rather than at its edge.

If you pad the zone instead, two things break. Your entry trigger becomes valid at 1.0897, which is below the actual base — you will be entering into a genuine breakdown while believing you are at the zone edge. And your recorded zone boundaries stop matching the price behaviour that created them, so when you review the trade later you cannot tell whether the zone worked.

Keep the zone honest. Put the tolerance in the stop, where it can be measured and where Module 9's position sizing will account for it.

EURUSD, London session. The reasoning is identical on index futures; only the units change.

3.4Fresh versus tested — the counter-intuitive one

Almost every retail source says a level that has held three times is stronger than one that has held once. This is backwards, and the reason it is backwards explains most of what you need to know about how zones work.

The mechanism

A zone works because unfilled orders rest there. Every test consumes some of them. A zone that has held three times has had three rounds of its inventory eaten. It is not stronger; it is emptier — and the diminishing size of each successive bounce is the market telling you so.

TouchTypical behaviourHow to treat it
First (fresh)Sharp reaction, often with displacement awayHighest-probability test. This is the one the system is built to catch.
SecondReaction still present but usually shallower and slowerTradable, but requires stronger 15M confirmation and a demonstrably clean structural stop.
ThirdWeak reaction, often just a pauseDemote. Watch only. Most breaks happen on the third or fourth attempt.
Fourth or moreUsually breaks throughNot a zone any more. Consider the opposite case: the repeated attempts have built a liquidity pool just beyond it.
Reading the bounce sizes is the skill

Do not count touches mechanically. Measure the reactions. Three touches producing 40, 38 and 41 pips of reaction is a genuinely well-defended area with two-sided interest. Three touches producing 40, 22 and 9 pips is a zone being consumed in front of you, and the next attempt is more likely to break than to hold. The sequence carries the information, not the count.

3.5The flip

When a zone is genuinely broken — closed through and accepted beyond — it frequently reverses role. Old resistance becomes support; old support becomes resistance. This is not mysticism, and the mechanism is worth stating precisely because it tells you when the flip will not happen.

Why the flip happens

Three groups act at the same price for different reasons

  • The trapped shorts. Sellers who entered at the zone while it was resistance are now in loss. On the retest they are back at break-even and many will close — which means buying.
  • The regretful buyers. Traders who watched the breakout and did not take it have been waiting for a pullback. The retest is the entry they wanted.
  • The breakout traders' stops. Those who bought the break placed stops just below the zone. Their stops are now resting sell orders below it — which is precisely why price often wicks slightly into or through the zone before turning.
The condition that makes a flip valid

Acceptance, not just a break. One candle closing beyond the zone is not enough. You want closes beyond it that hold — ideally with displacement through, then continued trade on the far side. A marginal close followed by an immediate return is a failed break (§3.7), and the zone has not flipped; it has been defended.

When the flip fails

Flips are unreliable when the break was slow and grinding rather than displaced, when the break happened in thin liquidity or on a news spike, and when price returns to the zone many sessions later. The population that gives the flip its mechanism — trapped traders, waiting buyers, resting stops — disperses over time. A flip zone retested within the same or next session is far more reliable than one retested a week on.

3.6Grading a zone before price arrives

The hardest part of using zones is not drawing them. It is refusing to re-evaluate them while price is moving toward them. The solution is to score every zone in advance, in writing, and to treat the score as fixed once price is within striking distance.

Applying the rubric — two worked examples

ZONE A — scores 6/6

Created by a four-candle displacement leg off the 4H chart. Untouched since creation. Sits exactly at the last 4H higher low. Equal lows 12 pips beneath it hold obvious sell-side liquidity. Width is 11 pips, so a structural stop 4 pips below still leaves room for 1:2 to the prior swing high. Verdict: trade it when Gates 1, 3, 4 and 5 open.

ZONE B — scores 2/6

Formed by a slow grind, not displacement. Third touch. Visible only on the 15M. Nothing structural nearby. No obvious liquidity beyond it. Width is 34 pips, so any structural stop destroys the R:R. Verdict: this is not a zone. It is a price where something once happened.

Codifying the rubric

Five of the six criteria are mechanical and belong in the Gate 1–3 scanner: displacement (body ratio and ATR test from Module 2), freshness (count of subsequent touches), origin timeframe, confluence (distance to nearest marked swing or session extreme), and width sanity (zone width against distance to the next structural target). Liquidity-beyond is partly mechanical — equal highs and lows are detectable — but judging whether a pool is obvious enough to matter stays manual. Keep the output as a ranked watchlist with scores attached. It must not place orders, and it must not collapse the six criteria into a single number you stop looking behind.

The score is a filter, not a forecast

A 6/6 zone is not 'likely to hold'. It is a zone where, if the other gates open, the trade is worth taking at the risk you have defined. Plenty of 6/6 zones fail. The point of the rubric is that when one fails you can see it was a well-constructed decision with a bad outcome — which is the only condition under which you can keep executing a positive-expectancy system through a losing streak.

Check your understanding
A 1H demand zone has held three times. Reactions measured 45 pips, 24 pips, and 8 pips. Price is approaching for a fourth time, and 4H structure is bullish. What is the correct read?

This is the touch-counting error, and the numbers in the question are there to disprove it. Counting touches says 'three holds, therefore strong'. Measuring them says something completely different: 45, then 24, then 8. Each defence was roughly half the previous one. That is a zone being consumed in front of you.

The mechanism from §3.4 explains why. A zone holds because unfilled orders rest there. Each test eats some of them. By the fourth approach the inventory that produced a 45-pip reaction has been substantially worked, and what remains produced only 8 pips last time.

The 4H bullish context does not rescue this. Gate 1 being open means longs are permitted — it says nothing about whether this specific location is still a location. Gate 2 is the one failing here, and gates are independent. A valid direction at a depleted zone is still a rejected trade.

There is also a hidden trap in the phrasing 'strong support'. Three visible touches at the same area is exactly what makes a level obvious to everyone watching — which means the stops of everyone who bought those three touches are now stacked just beneath it. That is a liquidity pool, and it is the most likely destination of the next move.

Correct, and for the right reason. The sequence 45 → 24 → 8 is the signal, not the count. Each successive defence is weaker, which is the observable signature of a zone whose resting inventory has been eaten. An 8-pip reaction is barely a reaction at all — on most FX pairs in London that is within normal two-way noise.

Demoting it is the correct action, and it is worth being precise about what demotion means. It does not mean 'flip to short'. 4H structure is bullish, so Gate 1 still forbids shorts. It means this zone no longer satisfies Gate 2, so no trade exists here in either direction, and your attention should move to the next zone down — which, if the fourth test breaks through, may well be where the real opportunity forms.

The forward-looking read is the valuable part. Three visible touches have stacked protective sell stops just below the zone. If price breaks through, sweeps that pool, and then reclaims the area with a 15M close back inside — that is a high-quality long setup at a genuinely fresh location, with 4H direction behind it. The depleted zone is not the trade. What happens beneath it might be.

This is the error the grading rubric in §3.6 exists to prevent. You already have the evidence you need: 45, 24, 8. Deferring the judgement to the moment price arrives does not add information — it removes your ability to use the information you have, because you will be evaluating a moving chart with a position-sized decision waiting on it.

'Judge it in real time' reliably becomes 'find a reason to take it'. Price will do something in the zone, some candle will look encouraging, and the prior three data points will quietly stop mattering. §3.6 said it directly: score the zone before price arrives, and treat the score as fixed once price is within striking distance. This is the situation that rule was written for.

There is a legitimate version of waiting, and it is worth separating: waiting for a different, better-defined event — a sweep of the stops below the zone followed by a 15M reclaim. That is not a real-time judgement call; it is a pre-specified condition with an entry, a stop and an invalidation you can write down now. Write it down now, then wait for it.

This combines two errors the course has already rejected, and the combination is worse than either. The first is the size-and-stop valve: Gate 2 has failed, and a failed gate is a rejection, never an adjustment. The second is the stop-tightening error from Module 1 — your stop is a classifier, not a risk dial. Moving it closer does not reduce risk; it raises the probability of being stopped out while your thesis is still intact, converting a smaller loss per trade into more losses.

Look at what a tight stop means here specifically. The zone has been tested three times, so protective stops from all three generations of buyers are stacked beneath it. A tight stop places you inside that cluster. You are not just accepting normal noise risk — you are positioned exactly where the market has the strongest mechanical incentive to trade next.

The R:R arithmetic also flatters you dishonestly. A tighter stop makes the ratio on paper look better, which is precisely the 'dishonest 1:2' Module 1 warned about: you have not moved right on the grid toward better reward, you have moved down it toward a lower win rate. The displayed number improves while the expectancy gets worse.

GBPUSD, London session. Note that GBPUSD's deeper normal sweeps make the tight-stop option in D even more damaging than it would be on EURUSD.

3.7Liquidity — why obvious levels get attacked

Module 1 named liquidity as one of the four location ingredients and Module 2 showed you failed breaks. Here is the full picture, because it changes how you read every obvious level on your chart.

Resting liquidityOrders sitting at a known price waiting to be filled. Chiefly: protective stops (which are market orders once triggered) and breakout entry orders. They cluster where levels are obvious, because obvious levels are where most participants place them.
The uncomfortable implication

The more obvious a level is, the more liquidity rests beyond it, and the more attractive it becomes as a target. Obvious levels are not protection. Placing your stop just beyond the most visible swing high on the chart puts it in the most crowded, most frequently attacked price on the chart.

Where liquidity pools — a checklist

Mark these on every chart before the session

  • Equal highs / equal lows — two or more pivots at essentially the same price. The strongest signature.
  • Obvious swing highs and lows — any pivot a reasonable trader would mark.
  • Session highs and lows — Asian range extremes are routinely taken during London; London's extremes during New York.
  • Prior day high / low / settlement — particularly on index futures, where they are institutionally referenced.
  • Round numbers — 1.1000, 4500.00. Not magic, but genuinely crowded because humans place orders there.
  • Trendline touches — where many traders have drawn the same diagonal, stops cluster just beyond it. This course does not trade trendlines, but you should know where other people's are.

How to tell them apart in real time

QuestionFalse breakoutGenuine breakout
Did a candle CLOSE beyond the level?No — wicks only, or one marginal close immediately reversedYes — decisive close, ideally two
Was there displacement through it?No — the move through is slow or spikyYes — large body, small wicks
What happened on the next candle?Closed back inside the rangeHeld beyond, or pulled back and held the level as support
What was just beyond the level?A visible liquidity pool — equal highs, obvious stopsOpen space, or the pool was already taken earlier
What time was it?Session open, news release, or thin hoursWithin the main session, no scheduled event
You cannot predict which one it will be

This is a classification framework applied after the candle closes, not a forecast. Anyone claiming to know in advance whether a break will hold is selling something. What the framework gives you is the discipline to wait for the close before acting — which is exactly what keeps you out of the false ones, at the cost of entering the genuine ones slightly later.

3.8Stacking zones across timeframes

You will often find a 15M zone inside a 1H zone inside a 4H zone. This is not three signals. It is one location described at three resolutions, and understanding that prevents a specific sizing error.

CORRECT USE

Nested zones let you enter with a tighter structural stop than the 4H zone alone would permit, because the 15M reaction area gives you a nearer, still-legitimate invalidation point. The improvement in R:R is real and comes from better resolution, not from wishful thinking.

INCORRECT USE

'Three timeframes agree, so this is a high-conviction trade — I'll double my risk.' The three zones are not three independent pieces of evidence; they are one piece of evidence viewed three ways. Treating correlated observations as independent is how position sizes get out of control.

The rule for nested zones

Use the widest zone to decide where you are allowed to look, the middle zone to satisfy Gate 2, and the narrowest to place the entry and measure the stop. One trade, one stop, one risk unit — regardless of how many timeframes agree.

Why this matters more than it sounds

If you have ever built a signal-combination model you will recognise the failure immediately: treating correlated features as independent evidence inflates your confidence estimate in exactly the way that produces oversized positions and unpleasant drawdowns. Multi-timeframe alignment is a textbook case — the 15M zone exists because the 1H zone does. The correlation is near one by construction. The correct treatment is to count it once and take the resolution benefit in the stop placement, not in the size.

3.9Where zone analysis fails

ConditionWhat goes wrongWhat to do instead
Too many zones drawnEvery price is inside some zone, so the concept stops discriminating. You will always find a reason to enter.Cap yourself at three to five zones per instrument per session, scored and ranked. Delete the rest.
Zones drawn after the factHindsight makes every reversal look like it came from a zone you would have drawn. You will overestimate the method's reliability.Draw zones before the session and timestamp them. Only pre-drawn zones count in your journal.
Trending markets with shallow pullbacksPrice never reaches your zones, and you either miss the whole move or chase it.Accept the miss. In strong trends the alternative — entering away from a zone — is the worst version of this system.
Very wide zonesA structural stop beyond a wide zone destroys R:R, so you are tempted to tighten it inside the zone.Reject the trade. A zone too wide to trade is still a correctly drawn zone; it is just not actionable today.
News-driven movesPrice slices through zones without reacting, because the participants who created them have repriced.Stand aside through scheduled releases and re-map zones afterwards. Pre-news zones are frequently invalid post-news.
Illiquid instruments or sessionsWicks are partly spread artefact, so zone edges derived from them are in the wrong place.Trade liquid instruments in their main session. This is an instrument-selection problem.
The honest limitation

Zones do not cause price to turn. They mark places where a turn has a plausible mechanism. A well-constructed 6/6 zone at a perfect location will sometimes be sliced straight through with no reaction whatsoever, and no amount of analysis would have told you in advance. This is why the stop is structural and the R:R minimum is 1:2 — the method survives being wrong regularly, which is fortunate, because it will be.

3.10Instrument and session caveats

InstrumentZone behaviourPractical adjustment
EURUSDTight, well-respected zones. Reaction areas are narrow and consistent. Sweeps beyond zone edges are typically shallow.Zones of 8–15 pips are normal on the 1H. A structural stop 3–5 pips beyond the zone edge is usually sufficient.
GBPUSDWider zones and materially deeper sweeps. The same structural quality of zone will see price trade further past the edge before reversing.Expect zones of 15–25 pips on the 1H, and allow more room beyond the edge. A stop that works on EURUSD is frequently too tight here.
ES (S&P 500 futures)Extremely structural. Prior day high, low and settlement act as reference zones in their own right. Overnight-session zones matter and should be mapped separately.Add prior-day levels and the overnight range to your zone map before the cash open. Value-area edges behave as zones.
NQ (Nasdaq futures)Faster and less respectful. More false breakouts at obvious levels, and displacement through zones is common.Weight the displacement criterion more heavily, and require stronger 15M confirmation. The same zone score means less here than on ES.
The session-mapping habit

Before every session, mark: the prior session's high and low, the current session's opening range once formed, and any equal highs or lows visible on the 1H. These are not zones in the four-source sense — they are liquidity references. They tell you where price is likely to be drawn, which is different from where it is likely to reverse, and confusing the two is a common and expensive error.

3.11The full concept map

ZoneFresh vs testedFlipLiquidity pool
WHATA price band with evidence of prior participationHow many times price has returned since creationA broken zone reversing its roleResting stops and breakout orders at an obvious price
WHY it mattersIt is the location that satisfies Gate 2Determines how much order flow is likely leftCreates fresh zones in the direction of the breakExplains sweeps, false breakouts, and where price is drawn
WHERE to lookDisplacement origins, reaction areas, pre-expansion bases, swing areasAny zone — count and measure the returnsImmediately after a break with acceptanceEqual highs/lows, session extremes, prior day levels, round numbers

3.12Vocabulary introduced in this module

ZoneA price band, with edges derived from specific candles, where there is evidence of prior participation and reason to believe unfilled orders remain.
Supply zone / demand zoneA zone above price expected to attract selling / below price expected to attract buying. The directional labels for the same construction.
Displacement originThe consolidation or candle cluster a displacement leg launched from. One of the four zone sources, and usually the highest quality.
Pre-expansion baseA tight consolidation immediately before a large directional move. Positions were accumulated across its whole range.
Fresh zoneA zone price has not returned to since it was created. Highest probability of reaction, because its order inventory is unspent.
Flip zoneA zone that has been broken with acceptance and now acts in the opposite role. Requires trapped participants to still be present, so it decays with time.
Resting liquidityProtective stops and breakout orders sitting at a known, obvious price. Becomes market orders when triggered, which is why sweeps move price so quickly.
Liquidity sweep / stop huntPrice trading beyond an obvious level to consume the resting orders, then reversing. Identified by a wick beyond with the close back inside.
AcceptancePrice closing beyond a level and continuing to trade there. The condition that distinguishes a genuine break from a sweep.
Zone scoreThe six-criterion rubric from §3.6, applied in writing before price arrives and treated as fixed once it does.
Deferred to later modules

The complete entry sequence → Module 4. Which candle formations count as confirmation → Module 5. Exact stop placement arithmetic and position sizing → Modules 6 and 9. You now have every term those modules assume about location.

3.13Practical work

Practical 3.1

The Zone Construction Drill

Time: ~2 hours · Tools: charting platform, no indicators

Procedure

  1. Open a 1H chart of your chosen instrument and scroll back two months.
  2. Find ten displacement legs using Module 2's four tests. For each one, mark the origin zone using the rules in §3.3 — write down the upper and lower edge prices and which candle each came from.
  3. For each zone, record whether price later returned, how many times, and the size of each reaction in pips or points.
  4. Score each zone retrospectively against the six criteria in §3.6, using only information available before price returned.
  5. Compare: did higher-scoring zones produce larger first reactions?

What you are learning: whether the rubric discriminates on your instrument. Ten zones is far too few to prove anything — Module 1's sample-size work applies here in full — but it is enough to build the habit of deriving edges rather than choosing them, which is the real objective.

Practical 3.2

The Pre-Session Zone Map

Time: 20 minutes per session × 10 sessions

Procedure

  1. Before your session opens, map the instrument: mark every zone that scores 4 or more, plus the prior session high and low and any equal highs or lows on the 1H.
  2. Cap yourself at five zones. If you have more, delete the lowest-scoring until five remain.
  3. Screenshot the map and timestamp it. This is the crucial step — it makes hindsight impossible.
  4. Trade nothing. At the end of the session, screenshot the same chart again and compare.
  5. Record for each zone: did price reach it? Did it react? Was the reaction proportional to the score? Did price react anywhere you had not marked — and if so, was there a zone you missed or was it genuinely unmarked?

What you are learning: calibration under honest conditions. The timestamped screenshot is what separates this from self-deception. Almost everyone who does this exercise discovers that their hit rate on pre-drawn zones is considerably lower than their remembered hit rate on post-drawn ones — and that the gap between the two is the size of their hindsight bias.

Practical 3.3

The Liquidity Audit

Time: ~90 minutes

Procedure

  1. On a 15M chart, find twenty instances where price wicked beyond an obvious swing high or low and closed back inside.
  2. For each, record: what was the obvious level? How far beyond did the wick go? What happened in the following five candles?
  3. Now find ten instances where price closed beyond the same kind of level and held. Record the same information.
  4. Compare the two sets. Specifically: how often was a sweep followed by a move in the opposite direction of at least twice the sweep depth?
  5. Add a permanent column to your journal: 'was a liquidity pool taken before entry?'

What you are learning: to see liquidity as structure rather than as an explanation applied after the fact. Most traders only notice sweeps when they get stopped out by one. This exercise makes the pools visible before price reaches them, which is the only point at which the knowledge is worth anything.

Required before Module 4

Practical 3.2 must be running. Module 4 is the complete entry sequence, and it assumes you arrive at each session with a pre-scored zone map. Without one you will be constructing locations in real time while price moves — which is precisely the condition the whole system is designed to avoid.

Check your understanding
Price breaks below an obvious 1H support zone on a single candle that closes 3 pips beneath it, during the first ten minutes of the London open. The next candle closes back inside the zone. What is your read?

This applies the close rule mechanically and ignores all three qualifiers around it. Yes, a candle closed beyond — but §2.5 addressed this exact case explicitly: a marginal close is weak evidence, not strong evidence, and two questions resolve it. Did the break show displacement? A 3-pip close beyond is by definition not displacement. Did the following candle hold beyond? No — it closed back inside.

Both qualifying tests fail, and the timing makes it worse. The first ten minutes of the London open is the single most common window for sweeps that reverse: the session opens, liquidity is briefly thin, obvious overnight levels get taken, and then real two-way flow arrives and prices back inside.

The practical cost is specific. Shorting the retest from below means selling into a zone that has just demonstrated it will defend itself, with a stop that must sit above the zone — above the very area buyers just proved they will act in. You would be positioned against demonstrated flow, at a level everyone can see, in the hour when reversals from overnight extremes are most common.

Correct, and every element of the scenario supports it. Take them in order. The close beyond was marginal — 3 pips, no displacement, so no evidence of aggression. The next candle closed back inside, which is the definition of a failed break rather than acceptance. And the timing is the London open, the highest-probability window for exactly this behaviour.

The mechanism is straightforward. An obvious 1H support zone has protective sell stops stacked beneath it, placed by everyone who bought it previously. Those stops are resting sell orders at a known price — a pool. Price traded down, filled them, and immediately recovered. The pool was the destination.

Now be precise about what you have and have not got. You have Gate 3 satisfied — liquidity has been taken — and evidence that Gate 2's location is still valid. You do not yet have Gate 1 confirmed (what is the 4H doing?), Gate 4 (no 15M closed-candle confirmation has been described), or Gate 5 (no R:R measured). 'A long setup may be forming' is exactly the right strength of claim.

One further benefit: the sweep low is now your structural reference. The stop goes below that, not below the zone edge — and because the pool beneath has been consumed, that stop is in a materially safer place than it was an hour ago.

Over-cautious in a way that costs you the trade. Waiting for a close above the top of the zone means waiting for price to travel the entire zone width — perhaps 15 or 20 pips — before you will form a view. By then the reaction is largely complete and your structural stop still has to sit below the sweep low, so you have given away a significant chunk of R:R for information you already had.

You did have it. The close back inside the zone is itself the evidence. That is the failed-break signature from §2.5 and §3.7, and it is not ambiguous: wick through, close back inside, at the session open, with no displacement. Calling that inconclusive treats 'I have not seen the outcome yet' as equivalent to 'the evidence is balanced'.

There is a correct version of your caution, and it is worth stating because the difference is small but decisive: you should not enter yet, because Gate 4 requires a 15M closed-candle confirmation and none has occurred. But 'do not enter yet' is not the same as 'form no view'. The view is: the zone held, the pool is gone, and a long is the only direction worth watching for. Hold the view, wait for the trigger.

You have half of a real principle and applied it to the wrong object. It is true that orders get consumed by interaction, and §3.4's fresh-versus-tested material is built on exactly that. But what was consumed here was the stop pool beneath the zone, not the demand within it. Those are different populations of orders sitting at different prices.

The evidence tells you which was hit. If the demand inside the zone had been consumed, price would have continued lower — that is what running out of buyers looks like. Instead price recovered and closed back inside within one candle, which says the opposite: buyers were present in size, and the dip beneath simply let them fill against the stops being triggered.

Applied consistently, your rule would also eliminate the highest-quality setup in this entire system. A sweep-and-reclaim is a zone that has just proven itself by absorbing an attack, with the liquidity that would otherwise have pulled price lower now removed. Treating every interaction as invalidation means you only ever trade untouched zones, and untouched zones by definition have no evidence of current defence.

The correct version: a zone is invalidated by acceptance through it — closes beyond that hold, ideally with displacement. Not by a wick.

Assume EURUSD. On GBPUSD the sweep would typically be deeper — perhaps 8–12 pips beyond — without changing the interpretation.

3.14Module summary

  1. A line is a guess; a zone is a record. You never choose a zone's width — you read it off the candles that made the level matter.
  2. Four sources of a legitimate zone: displacement origin, reaction area, pre-expansion base, swing area. Each gives specific edges from specific candles.
  3. Zones expire. Participants who created a zone do not stay interested forever, and a zone that has been traded through is stale.
  4. Fresh beats tested. Every touch consumes resting orders, so the third touch is weaker than the first. Measure the reactions, do not count the touches.
  5. Diminishing bounce sizes — 45, then 24, then 8 — are the market telling you the zone is being consumed.
  6. A broken zone frequently flips role, because trapped traders, waiting buyers and resting breakout stops all act at the same price. Flips require acceptance, not just a break, and they decay with time.
  7. Score every zone against six criteria before price arrives, and treat the score as fixed once price is close. The score is a pre-commitment device, not a probability.
  8. Liquidity rests where levels are obvious. The more obvious a level, the more attractive it is as a target — obvious levels are not protection.
  9. A wick beyond with the close back inside is a sweep. A close beyond with displacement that holds is acceptance. Only the second is a break.
  10. Nested zones across timeframes are one location at three resolutions, not three independent confirmations. Take the benefit in stop placement, never in position size.
  11. A zone too wide to trade is still a correctly drawn zone. Reject the trade rather than tightening the stop into the zone.
  12. Zones mark places where a turn has a plausible mechanism. They do not cause turns, and well-built zones fail regularly. That is what the structural stop and the 1:2 floor are for.
What Module 4 does with this

You now have direction (Module 2) and location (Module 3). Module 4 assembles them into the complete 15M entry model: the full thirteen-step sequence from 4H bias to filled order, in both long and short form, with the minimum conditions for validity, the conditions that strengthen a setup, and the conditions that force you to stand aside.
